Cross-cutting behaviours unchanged from the consolidation pass: the day-2 dependency graph adds per-dependency findings/unknowns, and the cleared-dependency registry (clearedRegistryVersion 0.1.0) means holding a major token no longer forces publishable=false. Two publishability changes, both from the dialect dictionary recognising guards that were previously unreadable: frax-share-fxs is now publishable (5 of its 6 blockers were contracts stating plainly that a guard had fired — OZ v3 AccessControl, Frax's own governance strings — and the sixth was Ripcord's own zero-valued argument coming back as 'ERC20: approve from the zero address'); paid-network-token-proxy-2 and ethena-susde remain BLOCKED, correctly, and were deliberately not unblocked for the demo. targets.label: weth9
targets.why: Canonical Wrapped Ether. Immutable since 2015 — no proxy of any kind, no owner, no privileged capability at all. The baseline 'nothing to see here' case.
targets.observed: hasCode=true, bytecodeSize=3124. All EIP-1967/EIP-1822/legacy proxy slots read zero. owner()/pendingOwner() both revert (no Ownable). proxy.pattern=not_a_proxy. powerHolders=[]. unknowns=[], errors=[].

exitWindow.why: CORRECT, and RE-CLASSIFIED ON DAY 5 without any change in what was observed. Through day 4 this read `no_rule_change_route_found`, a status that conflated 'no route was found' with 'no route exists'. Calibration showed that conflation was wrong on 2 of the 3 contracts it fired on (Balancer Vault, rETH), so the status was split: `immutable_within_checks` is now a POSITIVE claim that must be earned, and everything else falls through to `undetermined`. WETH9 earns it — no DELEGATECALL in the runtime bytecode, dispatcher decoded and all 11 selectors enumerated, none of the 14 authority-indirection getters resolving, no taxonomy capability matched, owner/pendingOwner/AccessControl all empty — and the report now carries that `basis[]` explicitly. The claim is still bounded by its `caveats[]`: 11 unmatched selectors were not evaluated for privilege, and a bespoke registry exposing no getter would be invisible. See docs/CALIBRATION.md §3.

targets.label: aave-pool-addresses-provider
targets.why: Aave v3's PoolAddressesProvider on mainnet. Not upgradeable itself; its own Ownable owner is 0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, which is itself a contract (Aave governance executor), not an EOA — reduced centralization risk by the day-1 signal we can actually check (full timelock-delay verification is explicitly day-4 scope, not claimed here).
targets.observed: hasCode=true. All EIP-1967/legacy proxy slots read zero (genuinely not upgradeable). owner()=0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, classified type=contract via getCode. KNOWN LIMITATION surfaced by this fixture: proxy.pattern comes back 'unknown', not 'not_a_proxy', because the contract's own bytecode contains a real DELEGATECALL opcode — not because it's a proxy, but because PoolAddressesProvider deploys child proxies via `new InitializableImmutableAdminUpgradeabilityProxy(...)`, and Solidity embeds that child contract's full initcode (including its real DELEGATECALL) inside the parent's own bytecode. Confirmed by finding a second '6080604052' contract-prologue signature embedded partway through the bytecode. Ripcord's bytecode scan is a linear walk (respecting PUSH-data lengths) with no control-flow reachability analysis, so it cannot distinguish 'opcode this contract would execute' from 'opcode embedded as another contract's creation code.' Documented as a known false-'unknown' in README Limitations rather than suppressed.

exitWindow.why: CORRECT, AND THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE MISS IN THE SET. The single authority route (owner) walks PoolAddressesProvider -> 0x5300A1a1 (Aave Governance v3 Executor) -> 0xdAbad81a (PayloadsController) -> 0xd3cf979e, terminating at max_depth. Verified live why no delay is found: the Aave v3 Executor exposes exactly FOUR selectors — executeTransaction / owner / transferOwnership / renounceOwnership — and NO delay accessor at all (getMinDelay, delay, getDelay, GRACE_PERIOD, getGracePeriod all revert). Aave keeps the delay in the PayloadsController, keyed by governance access level, which is a custom shape Ripcord does not recognise. An Aave-specific detector was deliberately NOT added: that is over-fitting to one protocol, and the honest 'undetermined' is the correct output for a custom timelock. Logged as KNOWN EDGE #17. Note the assessment is `undetermined`, not `not_proven_binding` — no route carries ANY delay, so there is nothing to be 'unproven' about, and using that label would imply a delay the evidence never found.

targets.label: paid-network-token-proxy-1
targets.why: One of two PAID Network (PAID) token proxies on mainnet, the protocol behind the well-documented March 2021 proxy-admin-key-compromise exploit (~$2.5-3M loss) — a textbook real-world instance of exactly the risk class Ripcord targets: audited code, no bug, an admin key change was enough. Illustrates the asymmetry directly: the token's own business-logic owner is a reasonably-configured 3-of-11 Gnosis Safe, but the separate, more powerful UPGRADE authority (the ProxyAdmin contract) is owned by a single EOA with no timelock — the more dangerous capability is the less protected one.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_transparent, implementation=0x3159810dd4d4d96961f3f04737d53650b6550690, admin=0x8f7e89f9017badba38d541b77e2e4073852d6b8b (an OpenZeppelin ProxyAdmin contract, selectors match ProxyAdmin.sol exactly: getProxyImplementation/upgrade/changeProxyAdmin/owner/transferOwnership). authority.owner=0x5f1bD0Feb0bF7C3ee0cde570f807436D29F4B4b2, classified type=safe, Gnosis Safe v1.1.1, threshold=3, 11 owners. Manually verified beyond day-1 scope (not something Ripcord itself resolves today — dependency-graph traversal through a ProxyAdmin's own owner() is explicitly day-2 scope): calling owner() on the ProxyAdmin (0x8f7e89f9017badba38d541b77e2e4073852d6b8b) itself resolves to 0x3cc21a33fe8ed011a307fd5988f6535bcb3f2ae3, which has no code (a plain EOA) — the true upgrade authority. Ripcord's day-1 output correctly and conservatively stops at classifying the direct admin as type=contract; it does not yet claim to know who controls that contract.

exitWindow.timeToExit: blocked — exit is HALTED at the pinned block
exitWindow.why: CORRECT, and the sharpest single-screen demonstration of the thesis in the set. Two routes, both zero-notice: proxyAdmin -> EOA 0x3CC21A33 (CODE_CHANGE) and owner -> a 3-of-11 Safe 0x5f1bD0Fe (AUTHORITY_CHANGE). The Safe is modelled as ZERO notice, which is the load-bearing modelling call of day 4: a threshold raises how many parties must agree and adds no time whatsoever, and the exit window measures time. Note the asymmetry the day-1 fixture already flagged is now quantified — the MORE powerful route (upgrade) is the LESS protected one (a single key, not the multisig). SEPARATELY, verified live by direct eth_call at this block: paused() == true on 0x1614f18f. Exit is not merely slow, it is currently halted, so time-to-exit is unbounded. The verdict therefore reports no_notice AND appends the halted-exit clause.

targets.label: paid-network-token-proxy-2
targets.disclosureNote: DAY 2: this is the DEPRECATED v1 token, superseded after the March 2021 exploit. Verified by deployment date via Ripcord's own findDeploymentBlock: this contract deployed at block 11724025 (2021-01-25, i.e. BEFORE the exploit), while paid-network-token-proxy-1 (0x1614...d787) deployed at block 12002538 (2021-03-09, i.e. IN the exploit window) and is therefore the post-incident redeploy. Both report totalSupply 594717455e18 and name/symbol 'PAID Network'/'PAID'. Day-2 guard probing observed that mint(address,uint256) does not revert when called from an unrelated address on this v1 contract (confirmed with realistic non-zero args, so not a zero-args artifact). Per the disclosure policy this was NOT investigated further for exploitability and is NOT published as a vulnerability claim: the report correctly routes it to needsManualVerification and its disclosure.publishable is false, so this fixture is excluded from the published calibration set. The contract is an abandoned pre-migration deployment with no current users, so there is no meaningful disclosure target. The PAID material used in the demo is the power asymmetry from the publicly documented 2021 incident, not this observation.
targets.why: The second PAID Network token proxy on mainnet — same protocol/incident as paid-network-token-proxy-1, but this one's own business-logic owner is directly a plain EOA (no multisig at all), making it the more starkly 'concerning' of the two: a fully single-key-controlled upgradeable token, both for business logic and (per manual follow-up) for upgrades.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_transparent, implementation=0xb828e66eb5b41b9ada9aa42420a6542cd095b9c7, admin=0x7bb7580edb70170daf8a24afc6aaef93db720c24 (ProxyAdmin contract, same selector signature as proxy-1's). authority.owner=0x53bc21D38281D6AcdFE0b92e0B534a19C90344cC, classified type=eoa directly (getCode returns empty). Manually verified beyond day-1 scope: the ProxyAdmin's own owner() resolves to 0x18738290af1aaf96f0acfa945c9c31ab21cd65be, also a plain EOA (no code) — so both the business-logic owner and (one hop past what Ripcord resolves today) the upgrade authority are single EOAs, no multisig, no timelock anywhere in the chain.

exitWindow.why: CORRECT. Both routes terminate at plain EOAs (proxyAdmin -> 0x18738290, owner -> 0x53bc21D3) with no delay anywhere, so the window is a PROVEN zero rather than an unknown. paused() reads false here (unlike proxy-1), so exit is not currently blocked. PROOF/VERDICT AGREEMENT: `ripcord prove` on THIS address produces a real drain against the resolved EOA (run it to see the figure; this report is stored as a `scan`, and the address is disclosure-BLOCKED so it has no published page — the project's headline dollar figure is Compound Comet's, never this one), and the proof carries noticeSeconds=0 — 'this authority is subject to NO notice period.' Proof and exit window state the same fact from two directions, which is the day-4 requirement that they agree structurally rather than by luck.

targets.label: wasabi-perp-manager
targets.why: Wasabi Protocol's PerpManager proxy on mainnet — the exact protocol and vulnerability class cited in this project's own brief: on 2026-04-30, an attacker took over the 'wasabideployer.eth' EOA, which held sole, unchecked admin authority (no multisig, no timelock) over every upgradeable Wasabi vault, and used it to UUPS-upgrade the perp vaults and LongPool to a malicious implementation, draining ~$4.5-5.9M across four chains in under three minutes. Chosen deliberately as the 'genuinely uncertain' fixture: Ripcord correctly identifies the proxy pattern (real evidence, real slots) but cannot identify the authority (also real, honest, evidence-backed non-detection) — demonstrating 'unknown is never safe' with a real incident rather than a contrived one.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_uups (implementation slot populated, admin slot zero), implementation=0xa8516ff9d132ed3a3c352fe04f05fe117bae97ce. owner() reverts (no Ownable). DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE() reverts, and hasRole(keccak256('ADMIN_ROLE'), wasabiDeployerEOA) also reverts — Wasabi does not implement OpenZeppelin's standard AccessControl interface at all; it uses a custom, unrecognised access-control scheme (independently reported as a single ADMIN_ROLE gate on the deployer EOA, but Ripcord's day-1 detectors have no evidence for this — deliberately not asserted in the report). Confirmed 0x5c629f8c0b5368f523c85bfe79d2a8efb64fb0c8 (the reported deployer/attack-vector EOA) has no code, independent of and prior to this fixture's inclusion. authority.owner=null, authority.accessControl.detected=false, powerHolders=[]. Because proxy.isProxy=true but no admin/owner/accessControl was found, build.ts emits an explicit unknowns[] entry (field='authority') stating the proxy IS upgradeable by someone unidentified — the report never lets 'found nothing' silently read as 'nothing to find.'

exitWindow.why: CORRECT — this is the 'unknown is never safe' case carried through to the metric. The target is a confirmed eip1967_uups proxy but no authority route resolves at all (custom access-control scheme, day-1 finding), so the exit window assessment is `undetermined` with the missing entry naming the exact problem: 'this contract is upgradeable, but the authority that can upgrade it was not identified.' The verdict refuses to compare rather than defaulting to a comforting number, which is the behaviour acceptance criterion 4 asks for. Proof engine also refuses (UUPS is outside the one implemented archetype) — both honesty signals agree that nothing can be established here.

targets.label: frax-share-fxs
targets.why: Added in the consolidation pass to exercise the OpenZeppelin AccessControl path, which NO prior fixture used — that gap is exactly what left KNOWN EDGE #7 (getLogs chunking) untested. FXS is a real, widely-held token that implements AccessControlEnumerable, and its DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE resolves (via the day-3 recursion) to a Frax multisig — a clean, honest 'privileged but multisig-guarded' case, and the fixture that proves the adaptive-getLogs + partial-reconstruction machinery against real on-chain state.
targets.observed: authority.accessControl.detected=true, method=enumerable. DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00..00) has exactly ONE member, 0xB1748C79709f4Ba2Dd82834B8c82D4a505003f27, independently verified live via getRoleMemberCount/getRoleMember (plain eth_calls, provider-independent). That member classifies as type=safe: a Gnosis Safe v1.3.0, threshold=3 of 5 owners (the Frax multisig) — so authorityResolution's [accessControl:DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE] path terminates as 'safe' with the threshold+owners recorded. findDeploymentBlock located FXS at block 11465584. RECONSTRUCTION LABEL (the point of the fixture): against the capped public provider (blastapi, probed eth_getLogs range = 9 blocks), the full deployment-to-pinned history (11465584..25800000, ~14.3M blocks) far exceeds the 1500-request budget, so role-HASH discovery covered only the most recent window (25793250..25800000) and the report labels reconstruction.complete=false, confidence=medium, with the exact covered window and an explicit unknowns[] entry — NOT a silent truncation. Enumerable membership is authoritative regardless, so DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE membership above is correct even under the partial scan; a role never touched in that recent window could be missed, which is precisely what the medium-confidence label warns. reconstruction.complete=true / confidence=high requires a provider whose probed getLogs range covers the full history within the 1500-request budget (~range >= history/750, i.e. ~19k blocks for FXS) — LARGER than Infura's 10k or Alchemy PAYG's 2k, so FXS stays a labelled partial even on those; an unbounded-range endpoint or a raised MAX_LOG_REQUESTS is what flips it. LIVE CROSS-PROVIDER CHECK (2026-09-01): re-ran on an Alchemy key (Free tier, also 10-block getLogs cap) — probed range 9, identical partial result (same covered window 25793250-25800000, same DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE member), confirming provider-independence of the reconstructed output; a fresh --no-cache Alchemy run of weth9 was byte-identical (minus generatedAt) to the blastapi-populated cache, confirming provider-independent caching. Note: over ~1500 capped getLogs calls the Alchemy free tier's rate limit produced a transient failure that fail-loud aborted the AC stage into errors[] on the first --no-cache pass; a cached re-run completed cleanly (see KNOWN EDGE #13). Full scan schema-valid at schemaVersion 0.6.0, errors=[], one unknowns[] entry (the partial-reconstruction label). disclosure.publishable=false because FXS's OWN capabilities (e.g. setOracle/revokeRole) route to needsManualVerification — the target's own findings always block, never cleared by the registry.

exitWindow.why: CORRECT, and it exercises the day-4 role-privilege gate in the POSITIVE direction. The single route is accessControl:DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE -> Safe 0xB1748C79 (3-of-5, the Frax multisig). The route is credited as `rolePrivilege: verified` because DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE administers every role by construction in OpenZeppelin AccessControl — not because of its name. It then resolves to a Safe, which imposes zero notice, so the window is a proven zero. A well-run multisig with no timelock is exactly this: a real collusion barrier and no time barrier at all, and the report says both.

targets.label: compound-comet-cusdcv3
targets.why: Added on day 4 because NONE of the original six fixtures had a genuine, un-shortenable timelock, and the brief requires at least one protocol where the window is real and binding. Compound III's USDC market is a large, live, EIP-1967 transparent proxy whose ProxyAdmin is owned by the Compound governance Timelock — the exact shape the day-4 binding machinery has to get right, and the counterweight to PAID's zero-notice case.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_transparent, implementation=0x83d491269720ce925f92c6bf9f66b7a0779a293a, admin=0x1EC63B5883C3481134FD50D5DAebc83Ecd2E8779 (Comet ProxyAdmin). ProxyAdmin.owner()=0x6d903f6003cca6255D85CcA4D3B5E5146dC33925, detected as a compound_bravo timelock: delay()=172800 (2 days), admin()=0x309a862bbc1a00e45506cb8a802d1ff10004c8c0 (GovernorBravo), GRACE_PERIOD()=1209600. All read live. The target's own governor() also reads 0x6d903f60, independently corroborating the resolved authority. Holds 39744687928433 USDC (~$39.7M) plus WETH and WBTC at this block. isWithdrawPaused()/isSupplyPaused()/isAbsorbPaused() all read false. DAY-4 BINDING PROBE (the point of the fixture): setDelay(uint256) called from an unrelated address reverts with Error(string) 'Timelock::setDelay: Call must come from Timelock.' — a self-call gate, so binding=proven_binding, method=self_call_gated_revert. detectProxy on the timelock itself returns not-a-proxy, so timelockIsUpgradeable=false. errors=[], unknowns=[], disclosure.publishable=true.

exitWindow.why: CORRECT — the healthy case, and the fixture that proves the binding machinery end to end. One route: proxyAdmin -> Comet ProxyAdmin 0x1EC63B58 -> owner -> Compound Timelock 0x6d903f60, detected as compound_bravo with delay() = 172800. Binding is established by PROBE, not by name: setDelay(uint256) reverts with 'Timelock::setDelay: Call must come from Timelock.' — a self-call gate, so the delay can only be changed by an operation the timelock schedules against itself, which is subject to the current delay. The timelock is also checked for being itself behind a proxy (it is not). Zero bypasses found, and 6 of 8 checks performed with the 2 skipped ones named. Comet withdrawal is synchronous and isWithdrawPaused() reads false, so exit is instant: 2 days of notice against a 0s exit.

targets.proofNote: THE DAY-4 PROOF/EXIT-WINDOW DISAGREEMENT, INVESTIGATED AND RESOLVED (acceptance criterion 5). `ripcord prove` on this target PRODUCES a proof: impersonating the resolved controller (the Compound Timelock) it upgrades the proxy to the drainer and moves $540,604,938.71 of USDC+WETH+WBTC. Taken alone that headline contradicts the healthy exit window — and the day-3 engine would have printed exactly that, because anvil impersonation executes AS the controller and therefore silently SKIPS the timelock queue that makes the timelock meaningful. The capability claim is true; presenting it without the notice period would have been the single most damaging overclaim available to this tool, against one of the best-governed protocols in the set. Fixed on day 4 rather than by refusing the proof (refusing would hide a real capability): the Proof schema gains noticeSeconds/noticeNote sourced from the exit-window ROUTE — one source of truth, so the proof and the verdict can never quote different delays — and the headline now ends '...This authority is subject to a proven-binding 172800s notice period, which the fork skips by impersonation — in reality the operation would be publicly visible for that long before it could execute.' The two signals now agree by construction.

targets.label: ethena-susde
targets.why: Added on day 4 as the fixture where the asymmetry actually BITES with both sides determined: a real, proven-binding 1-day timelock on the owner, against a real, readable 1-day exit cooldown. It is the only target in the set that produces a two-sided comparison with a computed margin, and the margin is exactly zero. It is also the fixture that caught the day-4 role-privilege false positive (see exitWindow.why), which makes it the most valuable target in the set for calibration purposes.
targets.observed: NOT a proxy (all EIP-1967/legacy slots read zero; 17299 bytes of code). owner()=0xe8dc0fab349ea169283c48ccfd09d797e6db7c94, which is an OpenZeppelin TimelockController: getMinDelay()=86400 (1 day), read live. That owner also holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on sUSDe (hasRole(0x00..00, owner) == true, verified live). AccessControl is present but NOT Enumerable (DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE() resolves; getRoleMemberCount reverts), so role membership comes from event reconstruction — a LABELLED PARTIAL on a range-capped provider, exactly as in the FXS fixture. cooldownDuration()=86400, MAX_COOLDOWN_DURATION()=7776000 (90 days), and the dispatcher (56 selectors) contains setCooldownDuration(uint24), cooldownShares(uint256), unstake(address), addToBlacklist(address,bool). Day-4 binding probe: updateDelay(uint256) on the timelock reverts Error(string) 'TimelockController: caller must be timelock' → proven_binding. errors=[], disclosure.publishable=false (renounceRole routes to needsManualVerification — the target's OWN capability, which the cleared registry never clears).

exitWindow.why: CORRECT, AND THE FIXTURE THAT SHAPED TWO DAY-4 RULES. (1) The owner route resolves to an OpenZeppelin TimelockController 0xE8Dc0Fab with getMinDelay() = 86400, PROVEN BINDING by probe: updateDelay(uint256) reverts 'TimelockController: caller must be timelock'. (2) cooldownDuration() reads 86400 and the exit is two-step (cooldownShares -> unstake), so leaving takes exactly as long as the notice you are guaranteed. That exact tie is why `trapped` uses >= and not >: you would finish exiting at the instant the change becomes effective, which is not exiting BEFORE it. marginSeconds is published as '0' so the dead heat reads as one. (3) THE FALSE POSITIVE THIS FIXTURE CAUGHT: three plain EOAs (0x8ED543D0, 0x8188af46, 0x1AdF6f82) hold role 0x0a4af4bc… = keccak256('FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE') — they are BLACKLISTED USERS, not administrators. The first day-4 run reported 'exit window is zero: 3 of 4 routes can change the rules with no notice' about three addresses that can change nothing. Membership was re-verified live via direct hasRole() calls (all three true, all three codeless), so the reconstruction was right and the INTERPRETATION was wrong. Fixed by the role-privilege gate (schema `rolePrivilege`): a role earns a place in the window arithmetic only if it is DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, administers another role, or has a capability guard attributed to it. These three are `unverified` and contribute `undetermined`, not a proven zero — which is also why the window assessment is `not_proven_binding` rather than `binding` even though the timelock itself IS proven binding. The verdict is still reachable because unresolved routes can only make the window SHORTER, and the exit already equals the longest resolved notice. NOTE also `mutableBy`: setCooldownDuration(uint24) is present in the dispatcher and MAX_COOLDOWN_DURATION() is 7776000 (90 days), so the 1-day exit is a privileged SETTING, not a protocol constant.

targets.disclosureNote: Everything reported about this target is documented, public protocol design: an owner-timelock, a staking cooldown, an owner-settable cooldown bounded by a published maximum, and role membership readable by anyone. Nothing here is a vulnerability claim; it is capability reporting in the project's usual sense — what a privileged address is technically able to do, with no assertion that anyone will do it. The report is nevertheless disclosure.publishable=false on the usual mechanical rule (an unattributed capability on the target itself), so it is excluded from any published calibration set regardless.
targets.runtimeNote: This fixture is the slowest in the set: sUSDe and its TimelockController are both non-Enumerable AccessControl, so each needs an event-reconstruction scan, and on a getLogs-range-capped provider that is ~1500 requests apiece. Day 4 added a bounded transient retry to the chain client (see KNOWN EDGE #13) after rate-limit failures aborted this scan twice; with it the scan completes in a single pass. Expect several minutes cold, instant warm.
